cls: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) analog / melanocortin receptor agonist
pharm: Pituitary hormone - stimulates adrenal cortex (repository corticotropin injection)
quick: Avoid unless clearly needed; teratogenic in animals
Caution; may suppress infant growth or interfere with endogenous steroid production
Use with caution; can cause fluid/electrolyte retention and hypertension
Use with caution; corticosteroid-type effects may be enhanced

summary: Repository corticotropin injection (ACTH gel) is a porcine adrenocorticotropic hormone analog that stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete cortisol, corticosterone, aldosterone and androgens, and also acts via melanocortin receptors. It is given IM or SC for acute exacerbations of multiple sclerosis, for infantile spasms (West syndrome) in infants and children under 2 years, and as adjunctive anti-inflammatory therapy in nephrotic, rheumatic, collagen, dermatologic, allergic, ophthalmic and respiratory disorders. Because its effects mimic chronic glucocorticoid excess, prolonged use causes adrenal suppression and Cushingoid effects, and therapy must be tapered rather than stopped abruptly.
indications: Treatment of infantile spasms (West syndrome) in infants and children under 2 years of age
Treatment of acute exacerbations of multiple sclerosis in adults
Adjunctive therapy for short-term administration in rheumatic disorders (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis)
Collagen diseases during an exacerbation or as maintenance (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic dermatomyositis)
Dermatologic diseases (e.g., severe erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
Allergic states (e.g., serum sickness, severe asthma unresponsive to conventional therapy)
Ophthalmic diseases (e.g., keratitis, iritis, optic neuritis, uveitis, allergic conjunctivitis)
Edematous states - to induce diuresis or remission of proteinuria in nephrotic syndrome without uremia of the idiopathic type or that due to lupus erythematosus

dosage.t: Twice daily for 2 weeks, then taper over 2 weeks
dosage.n: Taper: 30 units/m2 AM x3 days, then 15 units/m2 AM x3 days, then 10 units/m2 AM x3 days, then 10 units/m2 every other AM x6 days
May reduce dose gradually; individualize to disease severity and response
Adjust dose and interval by indication, disease severity and patient response; use lowest effective dose

dosage.d: Individualize per indication; consider full daily dose in first few days of acute conditions
dosage.n: When stopping after prolonged use, reduce dose gradually rather than abruptly

admin: Administer only by intramuscular or subcutaneous injection; intravenous administration is contraindicated
Warm the gel to room temperature before injection and use a dry needle and syringe to draw up the viscous repository preparation
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time consistent with the clinical situation
When discontinuing after prolonged therapy, taper the dose gradually to allow recovery of adrenal function
Do not administer live or live-attenuated vaccines during therapy because of immunosuppression
moa: Corticotropin is a purified porcine adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) analog that binds melanocortin receptors. At the adrenal cortex (MC2 receptor) it stimulates synthesis and secretion of endogenous corticosteroids - cortisol (hydrocortisone), corticosterone and aldosterone - as well as adrenal androgens, producing systemic glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid effects. Its therapeutic anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions in conditions such as multiple sclerosis exacerbations, nephrotic syndrome and infantile spasms are thought to derive both from increased endogenous steroid production and from direct melanocortin-receptor-mediated effects independent of cortisol. It is effective only when the adrenal cortex is functional and capable of responding.

absolute: History of or the presence of peptic ulcer
Sensitivity to proteins of porcine origin
Concomitant administration of live or live-attenuated vaccines
relative: Latent tuberculosis or positive tuberculin reaction
Diverticulitis, recent intestinal anastomoses, ulcerative colitis (perforation/abscess risk)
Psychiatric instability or history of psychosis
monitor: Signs of infection (effects may be masked)
Growth and development in infants and children

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Corticotropin has been shown to have an embryocidal effect and to cause increased fetal resorptions and abnormalities in animals. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus; infants born to mothers receiving the drug should be observed for signs of adrenal insufficiency.
lact: It is not known whether corticotropin is excreted in human milk; however, systemically administered corticosteroids appear in breast milk. Because of the potential to suppress growth, interfere with endogenous corticosteroid production, or cause other untoward effects in the nursing infant, decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, taking the importance of the drug to the mother into account.
renal: Use with caution in patients with renal insufficiency. The mineralocorticoid effect can cause sodium and fluid retention, edema, potassium loss and hypertension, which may worsen renal status; monitor blood pressure, weight and electrolytes.
hepatic: Use with caution; the effects of corticotropin may be enhanced in patients with cirrhosis or hypothyroidism. Monitor for exaggerated corticosteroid-type effects.

major: Live or live-attenuated vaccines - immunosuppression may reduce vaccine response and increase risk of disseminated infection (contraindicated)
Other immunosuppressants - additive immunosuppression and infection risk
moderate: Diuretics (thiazides, loop) and amphotericin B - additive hypokalemia
Cardiac glycosides (digoxin) - hypokalemia potentiates glycoside toxicity
Insulin and oral hypoglycemics - reduced glucose control (hyperglycemia)
NSAIDs/aspirin - increased risk of GI ulceration and bleeding
minor: Potassium-depleting agents in general - monitor serum potassium
interactions.food: Not applicable for the injection; a sodium-restricted, potassium- and protein-rich diet may be advisable during therapy.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; it adds to the risk of peptic ulceration and GI bleeding associated with corticosteroid effects.
interactions.diagnostics: Suppresses reactions to skin tests; may mask signs of infection; alters serum electrolytes and glucose. The drug stimulates endogenous cortisol, which will alter cortisol-based testing.

serious: Adrenal suppression / adrenal insufficiency on withdrawal
Increased susceptibility to and masking of infections
Growth suppression in infants and children
Peptic ulceration with possible perforation and hemorrhage
Congestive heart failure in predisposed patients
emergency: Anaphylaxis / severe hypersensitivity to porcine protein
Acute adrenal crisis after abrupt withdrawal

monitoring: Blood pressure, body weight and signs of fluid retention/edema
Signs and symptoms of infection (which may be masked)
Growth and development in infants and children on prolonged therapy
Bone density, ophthalmic exam (cataracts/glaucoma) and mood/behavior with prolonged use
Adrenal function and signs of insufficiency during and after withdrawal
counsel: This medicine is given as an injection under the skin or into a muscle - never into a vein
Do not stop the medicine suddenly; the dose must be reduced gradually as directed by your doctor
Report fever, sore throat or other signs of infection, as the drug can hide and worsen infections
Tell your doctor about mood changes, severe stomach pain, black stools, or marked swelling/weight gain
Avoid live vaccines and contact with people who have chickenpox or measles while on treatment
Carry a card or wear identification stating you are receiving corticotropin/steroid therapy
For infantile spasms, follow the exact tapering schedule and keep all follow-up appointments
pk: Adrenal cortisol response within hours; clinical effect over days
Plasma cortisol rises and peaks within a few hours of injection
ACTH plasma half-life approximately 15 minutes; repository (gel) prolongs absorption/effect
Prolonged corticosteroid stimulation over many hours due to the repository (gel) formulation
Store refrigerated at 2-8 C (36-46 F); do not freeze
pearls: Works only with a responsive adrenal cortex - it stimulates endogenous cortisol rather than supplying steroid directly, so it is ineffective in primary adrenal insufficiency

Long-term effects mirror chronic glucocorticoid/corticosteroid excess: adrenal suppression, Cushingoid changes, immunosuppression/infection, hyperglycemia, hypertension, hypokalemia, osteoporosis, growth suppression in children, mood changes, cataracts/glaucoma and GI ulceration
Always taper - never stop abruptly after prolonged use, to avoid acute adrenal insufficiency
Contraindicated for IV use and with live vaccines; derived from porcine protein, so avoid in pork-protein sensitivity
First-line option for infantile spasms (West syndrome) with a defined high-dose then tapering regimen
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time; supplement with diet measures (sodium restriction, potassium, protein) as needed
missed: If a scheduled dose is missed, contact the prescriber for guidance; do not double the dose. Because therapy relies on a defined schedule and tapering plan (especially in infantile spasms), missed doses should be reported so the schedule can be adjusted and abrupt discontinuation avoided.
overdose: Overdose produces effects of excess corticosteroid/mineralocorticoid activity - fluid retention, edema, hypertension, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia and Cushingoid manifestations. There is no specific antidote; discontinue or reduce the drug and treat supportively, correcting fluid and electrolyte imbalances (especially potassium) and managing hyperglycemia and hypertension. Monitor for and manage adrenal suppression.
